objective: Slicing the Circle. We begin by imagining the circle as made of many thin concentric rings, like tree rings or an onion. As you drag the radius outward, watch each ring appear — the circle isn't one solid shape, but layers stacked from the center out

finalists.title: Reverse-Engineer the Circle's Area Coverage
finalists.narrative_wrapper: You see a circle already divided into concentric rings, with a number showing its total area. Drag that area number up or down — as you increase the area, the circle physically grows and new rings appear at the boundary; as you decrease it, rings peel away from the outside. You're controlling the outcome (area) and watching the circle solve backwards to show you how many rings it needs.
finalists.manipulated_variable: The displayed total area value (A), which the student drags vertically or horizontally to increase/decrease
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: The circle itself grows or shrinks in real-time, with concentric rings appearing sequentially from the outside inward (when area increases) or disappearing from outside inward (when area decreases); the current radius value updates to show r = √(A/π)
finalists.goal_structure: Free exploration with optional suggested targets: 'Make the area exactly 50 square units' or 'How many rings fit when A = 100?'
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: Live display of: current area A being manipulated, computed radius r = √(A/π), number of rings visible N (quantized from r), and the outermost ring position matching the computed radius; a formula bar shows A = πr² with current values substituted
finalists.trace_strategy: Ghost outlines of previous circle sizes fade slowly, leaving a visual history of different area configurations and showing that larger areas always mean more rings from center outward
finalists.aha_moment: Realizing that area isn't arbitrary — it forces a specific radius and therefore a specific number of rings; the circle's layered structure is determined by working backwards from total area, revealing that A = πr² means 'this much area requires exactly this many layers out to this radius'
finalists.feasibility_sketch: The core primitives needed are draggable UI elements and dynamic SVG/canvas rendering of concentric circles, with no significant runtime risk.
finalists.weakness: The biggest weakness is the potential for cognitive overload if too many rings change too quickly without clear pacing or guidance.

finalists.title: Drag Radius to Grow Concentric Rings
finalists.narrative_wrapper: You see a circle's center point with a draggable radius line. As you drag the radius outward from zero, thin colored rings appear one by one, building up the full circle. The circle fills from inside out, revealing its layered structure.
finalists.manipulated_variable: Dragging the endpoint of a radius line outward from the center, which changes the current radius value r
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: Concentric rings appear sequentially inside the swept area, with each new ring appearing at the current radius position as the handle moves outward
finalists.goal_structure: Free exploration with optional encouragement to drag fully from center to edge to see the complete decomposition
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: The current radius value r displayed numerically, the number of rings shown so far, and optionally the thickness of each ring (dr) labeled on one ring
finalists.trace_strategy: All previously-drawn rings remain visible and accumulate, creating a full disk; no erasure occurs because the concept requires seeing the complete buildup of layers
finalists.aha_moment: The circle isn't a solid blob but rather dozens or hundreds of thin rings stacked together, each contributing a small amount to the total area
finalists.feasibility_sketch: Draggable SVG/canvas shapes with live readouts for radius and ring count; no significant runtime risk.
finalists.weakness: The narrative integration is weak, as the interaction lacks a clear build-up or narrative beats beyond the initial exploration.

narrative_draft.text:
We usually think of a circle's area as something we *calculate* — plug the radius into πr² and out pops a number. But what if we flip that around? What if you already know the area you want, and the circle has to figure out how big to be?

Try dragging the area value itself — up to increase it, down to shrink it. Watch what happens at the boundary. As the area climbs, the circle doesn't just inflate like a balloon; new rings emerge at the outer edge, one after another, building outward from the center. Drop the area back down and those same rings peel away in reverse. The circle is solving backwards: given this much area, exactly this many rings must fit, stretched out to exactly this radius. The formula r = √(A/π) isn't just algebra — it's the circle showing you its only possible configuration for that area.

This reversal reveals something profound. Area isn't a consequence of stacking rings to a chosen radius; the rings *are* the area, and demanding a specific total area forces a specific radius into existence. When you see the rings appear and vanish in lockstep with the area number, you're watching the deep symmetry inside πr² — area, radius, and the number of concentric layers are three faces of the same geometric truth.
